Staid

stayd (rhymes with 'made') · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Staid is quiet, serious, and respectably conventional in behavior or appearance.

The staid old bank building, with its dark wood paneling and hushed lobby, hadn't changed its decor in fifty years.

Worked Example

Even after winning the lottery, Mr. Alvarez remained entirely staid, still wearing the same gray suit and eating lunch at the same diner every day.

Staid doesn't mean sad or dull exactly -- it means someone (or something) that stays serious, steady, and properly composed, even when circumstances change.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

sober: serious and free from excess or exaggeration

decorous: correct and dignified in behavior

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

flashy: showy; attracting attention

rowdy: noisy and disorderly

Where it sits · how set in serious old ways — conventional → staid → stodgy

conventional vs. staid: Conventional just means following ordinary customs, without the extra weight of old-fashioned seriousness that staid implies.

stodgy vs. staid: Stodgy pushes staid's seriousness even further into dull, resistant-to-change territory.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — stay(ed)

root — stay(ed): settled, fixed in place or character (Middle English steyen, ultimately Latin stare, 'to stand')

Put it together

Put it together: Staid is literally an old form of 'stayed,' the past tense of stay. Both stay and staid trace back through Old French to the Latin root stare, 'to stand' -- the same ultimate root behind words like stable and static.

Use the root in a new word: stable

Use the root in a new word: stable: The old stone bridge had remained stable for three hundred years despite countless floods.

Root Check

Word Choice

Staid describes a person, place, or style that's seriously proper and unchanging -- often with a hint that it's a little dull. This unit also teaches sedate (calm and dignified, more about pace than personality) and prim (stiffly, almost fussily proper) -- staid is the most general of the three, describing an overall steady, serious character.
